claim: TKO-Bcl2 MEFs ceased proliferation upon mitogen deprivation.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Foijer et al., 2005), mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEFs) lacking the three retinoblastoma proteins and overexpressing the anti-apoptotic gene Bcl2 (TKO-Bcl2 MEFs) ceased proliferation upon mitogen deprivation (Figure 1A, black line)
evidence: Supported by growth curve data in Figure 1A showing TKO-Bcl2 cells stop proliferating without serum, and cited previous work (Foijer et al., 2005)

claim: TKO-Bcl2 MEFs arrested in a G2-like state upon mitogen deprivation.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Foijer et al., 2005), mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEFs) lacking the three retinoblastoma proteins and overexpressing the anti-apoptotic gene Bcl2 (TKO-Bcl2 MEFs) ceased proliferation upon mitogen deprivation (Figure 1A, black line) and arrested in a G2-like state (Figure 1C, upper panel).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle distribution data in Figure 1C showing accumulation in G2/M phase, and cited previous work (Foijer et al., 2005)

claim: Proliferation of mitogen-starved TKO-p53RNAi MEFs was transient and followed by severe cell loss.
source: However, in recent experiments, proliferation of mitogen-starved TKO-p53RNAi MEFs appeared transient and was followed by severe cell loss (Figure 1A, green line), possibly as a result of residual p53 activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data in Figure 1A showing initial proliferation followed by decline, and Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing residual p53

claim: Disruption of p53 rescued proliferation of mitogen-starved TKO MEFs.
source: Disruption of p53 clearly rescued proliferation of mitogen-starved TKO MEFs (TKO-p53KO) and this effect was even greater in TKO MEFs expressing Bcl2 (TKO-Bcl2-p53KO), which reached 100% confluency (Figure 1A, blue and red lines).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data in Figure 1A showing TKO-p53KO and TKO-Bcl2-p53KO cells proliferate without serum

claim: Improved proliferative capacity upon p53 knockout was accompanied by reduced apoptosis.
source: The improved proliferative capacity was accompanied by reduced apoptosis (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by apoptosis measurement data in Figure 1B showing lower caspase activity in p53KO cells

claim: Improved proliferative capacity upon p53 knockout was accompanied by the absence of G2 arrest.
source: The improved proliferative capacity was accompanied by reduced apoptosis (Figure 1B) and the absence of G2 arrest (Figure 1C, lower panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle distribution data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing normal cell cycle profile in p53KO cells without serum

claim: Mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO cells maintained a cell cycle profile similar to cells cultured in the presence of mitogens.
source: Mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO cells maintained a cell cycle profile similar to cells cultured in the presence of mitogens (Figure 1C, lower panel)
evidence: Supported by cell cycle distribution data in Figure 1C comparing serum-starved and serum-replete conditions

claim: TKO-Bcl2-p53KO cells continued to incorporate high levels of nucleotides upon mitogen deprivation, unlike TKO-Bcl2 cells.
source: Mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO cells maintained a cell cycle profile similar to cells cultured in the presence of mitogens (Figure 1C, lower panel) and, unlike TKO-Bcl2 cells, continued to incorporate high levels of nucleotides (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation data in Figure 1D showing maintained BrdU labeling in p53KO cells

claim: Disruption of Cdkn1a rescued proliferation of mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 cells.
source: Not only loss of p53, but also disruption of its downstream target Cdkn1a, the gene that encodes the p21Cip1 protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), rescued proliferation of mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data in Figure 1E showing TKO-Bcl2-p21KO cells proliferate without serum, and Western blot in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C confirming p21 knockout

claim: Induction of p21Cip1 upon mitogen deprivation was critical for G2-like arrest of mitogen-deprived TKO cells.
source: Apparently, the induction of p21Cip1, which we previously found to inhibit Cyclin A- and B1-dependent kinases (Foijer et al., 2005), was critical for G2-like arrest of mitogen-deprived TKO cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p21 knockout rescues proliferation, combined with previous findings (Foijer et al., 2005) about p21's role in inhibiting CDKs

claim: The p53/p21Cip1 axis is part of the DNA damage response.
source: The p53/p21Cip1 axis is part of the DNA damage response (DDR) and its activation is consistent with the high levels of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) that accumulated in arrested TKO-Bcl2 cells (van Harn et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and cited previous work (van Harn et al., 2010) showing DSB accumulation

claim: High levels of DNA double-strand breaks accumulated in arrested TKO-Bcl2 cells.
source: The p53/p21Cip1 axis is part of the DNA damage response (DDR) and its activation is consistent with the high levels of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) that accumulated in arrested TKO-Bcl2 cells (van Harn et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (van Harn et al., 2010)

claim: In the presence of mitogens, TKO-Bcl2 and TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs proliferated with a cell-cycle duration of 10 to 15 hr.
source: In the presence of mitogens, TKO-Bcl2 and TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs proliferated with a cell-cycle duration of 10 to 15 hr (Figure 2A,B, left).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 2A,B showing cell cycle timing

claim: In the absence of mitogens, TKO-Bcl2 MEFs arrested in S/G2 phase, either immediately or after one cell cycle.
source: In the absence of mitogens, TKO-Bcl2 MEFs arrested in S/G2 phase, either immediately or after one cell cycle (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 2A showing arrest patterns

claim: Mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs could be followed for two or three cell divisions.
source: In contrast, mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs could be followed for two or three cell divisions (Figure 2B, right), although G1 and S/G2 phase durations were increased, together encompassing 15 to 30 hr.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 2B showing multiple divisions

claim: G1 and S/G2 phase durations were increased in mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs, together encompassing 15 to 30 hr.
source: In contrast, mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs could be followed for two or three cell divisions (Figure 2B, right), although G1 and S/G2 phase durations were increased, together encompassing 15 to 30 hr.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 2B showing extended cell cycle phases

claim: TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs can proliferate in the absence of mitogens albeit at slower pace.
source: These tracking experiments confirm that TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs can proliferate in the absence of mitogens albeit at slower pace.
evidence: Inferred from the time-lapse data showing continued but slower cell divisions

claim: Mitogen restriction of TKO-Bcl2 MEFs caused a clear increase in tail moment.
source: Mitogen restriction of TKO-Bcl2 MEFs caused a clear increase in tail moment, an indicator of the level of DSBs (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 3A,B showing increased tail moments

claim: The tail moments in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO and TKO-Bcl2-p21KO MEFs were not significantly increased by mitogen depletion.
source: In contrast, the tail moments in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO and TKO-Bcl2-p21KO MEFs were not significantly increased by mitogen depletion (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 3B showing no significant increase in tail moments

claim: The basal levels of DSBs in the presence of mitogens were somewhat higher in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO and TKO-Bcl2-p21KO MEFs compared to TKO-Bcl2 cells.
source: In contrast, the tail moments in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO and TKO-Bcl2-p21KO MEFs were not significantly increased by mitogen depletion (Figure 3B) although the basal levels of DSBs (i.e., in the presence of mitogens) were somewhat higher compared to TKO-Bcl2 cells.
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 3B comparing baseline tail moments

claim: MEFs may accumulate some DNA damage under optimal culture conditions that was tolerated or not adequately repaired in the absence of p53/p21Cip1 activity.
source: Possibly, MEFs accumulated some DNA damage under optimal culture conditions that was tolerated or not adequately repaired in the absence of p53/p21Cip1 activity (Levine and Oren, 2009; Williams and Schumacher, 2016).
evidence: Speculative explanation for higher baseline DSBs, supported by citations (Levine and Oren, 2009; Williams and Schumacher, 2016)

claim: The induction of DNA breakage due to mitogen deprivation was suppressed in the absence of p53/p21Cip1.
source: Nevertheless, the critical observation here is that the induction of DNA breakage due to mitogen deprivation was suppressed in the absence of p53/p21Cip1.
evidence: Inferred from comet assay data showing no increase in DSBs upon mitogen deprivation in p53KO and p21KO cells

claim: Mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs showed the expected increase in tail moment in the presence of nocodazole.
source: In the presence of nocodazole, the same results were obtained: mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs showed the expected increase in tail moment, while the tail moments of TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs were still not increased (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 3C with nocodazole treatment

claim: The tail moments of TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs were not increased in the presence of nocodazole and mitogen deprivation.
source: In the presence of nocodazole, the same results were obtained: mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs showed the expected increase in tail moment, while the tail moments of TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs were still not increased (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 3C with nocodazole treatment

claim: Treatment with 2 mM hydroxyurea for 1 hr induces stalling and collapsing of replication forks and DNA breakage.
source: HU depletes the cells of nucleotides, which results in stalling and collapsing of replication forks and hence DNA breakage (Bianchi et al., 1986; Koç et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations (Bianchi et al., 1986; Koç et al., 2004)

claim: An equally strong decrease in tail moment was observed in TKO-Bcl2 and TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs 30 min after HU treatment compared to immediately after HU treatment.
source: When comparing cells harvested immediately after HU treatment and cells harvested 30 min after HU treatment, we observed an equally strong decrease in tail moment in TKO-Bcl2 and in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 3D showing similar repair kinetics

claim: The repair of DSBs induced by HU treatment was independent of p53 status.
source: This indicates that the repair of DSBs induced by HU treatment was independent of p53 status.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both cell types showed equal decrease in tail moment after HU treatment

claim: Reduced levels of DSBs in mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO cells resulted from suppressed formation rather than increased repair of DSBs.
source: Assuming that repair of replication-stress-induced DSBs under mitogen-deprived conditions follows similar rules, these results suggest that reduced levels of DSBs in mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO cells resulted from suppressed formation rather than increased repair of DSBs.
evidence: Inferred from the HU repair experiment showing p53-independent repair, combined with reduced DSB levels in p53KO cells

claim: The number of cells containing CldU foci gradually decreased in mitogen-starved TKO-Bcl2 MEFs.
source: While the number of cells containing CldU foci gradually decreased in mitogen-starved TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, virtually all CldU foci that were still present after 4 and 7 days co-localized with γ-H2AX foci (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A,B showing decreasing CldU-positive cells

claim: Virtually all CldU foci that were still present after 4 and 7 days of mitogen starvation co-localized with γ-H2AX foci in TKO-Bcl2 MEFs.
source: While the number of cells containing CldU foci gradually decreased in mitogen-starved TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, virtually all CldU foci that were still present after 4 and 7 days co-localized with γ-H2AX foci (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A,B showing co-localization

claim: The gradual increase of phosphorylated Chk1 is indicative for accumulation of single-stranded DNA.
source: Furthermore, the gradual increase of phosphorylated Chk1 (pChk1), a target of ataxia telangiectasia related (ATR), is indicative for accumulation of single-stranded DNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 4C showing increased pChk1, and established knowledge that pChk1 indicates ssDNA accumulation

claim: Co-localization of CldU and γ-H2AX foci and increased pChk1 are indicative for perturbed replication in mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs.
source: Taken together, these results are indicative for perturbed replication in mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of CldU/γ-H2AX co-localization and pChk1 increase

claim: The average fork speed in TKO-Bcl2 MEFs cultured with FCS was 1.66 kb/min.
source: The length of double-labelled tracks in TKO-Bcl2 MEFs cultured with FCS indicated an average fork speed of 1.66 kb/min (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5B measuring track lengths

claim: The average fork speed in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs cultured with FCS was 1.37 kb/min.
source: In the absence of p53 the average fork speed was somewhat lower, 1.37 kb/min, consistent with a previous study (Klusmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data and citation to previous study (Klusmann et al., 2016)

claim: Mitogen deprivation caused a progressive decline in replication speed in TKO-Bcl2 MEFs.
source: Mitogen deprivation caused a progressive decline in replication speed, somewhat unexpectedly not only in arresting TKO-Bcl2 MEFs but also in proliferating TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5B showing decreased fork speeds over time

claim: Mitogen deprivation caused a progressive decline in replication speed in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs.
source: Mitogen deprivation caused a progressive decline in replication speed, somewhat unexpectedly not only in arresting TKO-Bcl2 MEFs but also in proliferating TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5B showing decreased fork speeds over time

claim: Prolonged S-phase and decelerated DNA synthesis indicate that mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs were able to proliferate despite sustained replication stress.
source: Prolonged S-phase and decelerated DNA synthesis indicate that mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs were able to proliferate despite sustained replication stress.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of continued proliferation (Figure 1, 2) and reduced replication speed (Figure 5B)

claim: Mitogen-deprivation of TKO-Bcl2 cells reduced transcript levels of Ppat, Impdh1 and Impdh2 2-fold.
source: Indeed, we found that mitogen-deprivation of TKO-Bcl2 cells reduced transcript levels of phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate amidotransferase (Ppat) and inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (Impdh1 and Impdh2), genes involved in purine metabolism, 2-fold (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by transcript level data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: RNAi-mediated suppression of Ppat expression reduced the replication speed in mitogen-stimulated TKO-Bcl2 MEFs from 1.25 kb/min to 0.84 (shRNA #1) and 0.86 (shRNA #2) kb/min.
source: Indeed, RNAi-mediated suppression of Ppat expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) reduced the replication speed in mitogen-stimulated TKO-Bcl2 MEFs from 1.25 kb/min to 0.84 (shRNA #1) and 0.86 (shRNA #2) kb/min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and knockdown confirmation in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Replication speed in mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs could be partially rescued by the exogenous supply of nucleosides.
source: Conversely, replication speed in mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs could be partially rescued by the exogenous supply of nucleosides. Similar to previous experiments, one day of mitogen deprivation decreased the average fork speed by ±30%, in this experiment from 0.94 kb/min to 0.65 kb/min. In contrast, when cells were supplemented with nucleosides, reduction of replication speed was less pronounced (from 1.03 kb/min to 0.83 kb/min) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D comparing with and without nucleoside supplementation

claim: Daily nucleosides supplementation did not alleviate the proliferation defect of mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs.
source: However, daily nucleosides supplementation did not alleviate the proliferation defect of mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs: G2 accumulation was hardly affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) and also Chk1 phosphorylation and p21Cip1 induction were not reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F

claim: Mitogen-independent proliferation upon p53 loss did not require restoration of replication speed.
source: As we observed that mitogen-independent proliferation upon p53 loss did not require restoration of replication speed (Figure 5B), this indicates that rather than decelerated DNA replication another factor was causal to G2 arrest upon mitogen deprivation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p53KO cells proliferate despite reduced replication speed (Figure 5B)

claim: Among CldU/IdU-labelled DNA fibers from mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, staining patterns indicative for new origin firing were significantly reduced.
source: Indeed, among CldU/IdU-labelled DNA fibers from mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, staining patterns indicative for new origin firing were significantly reduced (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5C showing reduced origin firing

claim: In TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs, origin firing was not disturbed during the first days of mitogen deprivation and maintained levels similar as in mitogen-stimulated cells.
source: In contrast, in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs, origin firing was not disturbed during the first days of mitogen deprivation and maintained levels similar as in mitogen-stimulated cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5C showing maintained origin firing

claim: After 5 days of mitogen deprivation, origin firing was reduced in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs, which may be related to the state of confluency.
source: Only after 5 days of mitogen deprivation, origin firing was reduced, which may be related to the state of confluency that was reached by that time (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5C and growth curve data in Figure 1A, with speculative explanation

claim: TKO-Bcl2-p21KO MEFs maintained normal origin firing during the first days of mitogen deprivation.
source: Similar to TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs, also TKO-Bcl2-p21KO MEFs maintained normal origin firing during the first days of mitogen deprivation (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5C showing maintained origin firing

claim: Loss of p53 reduced the level of origin firing upon treatment with 300 µM HU.
source: Consistent with Roy et al., loss of p53 reduced the level of origin firing upon treatment with 300 µM HU.
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and consistency with cited work

claim: Loss of p53 did not change the level of origin firing after treatment with 2 mM HU.
source: However, loss of p53 did not change the level of origin firing after treatment with the high dose of HU (2 mM) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: Under conditions of severe replication stress, restoration of the level of origin firing upon p53 loss prevents DNA breakage, allowing mitogen-independent proliferation of TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that under conditions of severe replication stress, restoration of the level of origin firing upon p53 loss prevents DNA breakage, allowing mitogen-independent proliferation of TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of restored origin firing, reduced DSBs, and continued proliferation in p53KO cells

claim: In the presence of mitogens, TKO and CyclinD1 RPE-1 cells proliferated faster than wild type RPE-1s.
source: In the presence of mitogens, TKO and CyclinD1 RPE-1 cells proliferated faster than wild type RPE-1s (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: 24 hr after mitogen-deprivation, wild type RPE-1s arrested in the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
source: 24 hr after mitogen-deprivation, wild type RPE-1s arrested in the G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by cell cycle distribution data in Figure 6C

claim: TKO and CyclinD1 RPE-1 cultures maintained a normal cell cycle profile up to 72 hr after mitogen deprivation.
source: 24 hr after mitogen-deprivation, wild type RPE-1s arrested in the G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 6C), whereas both, TKO and CyclinD1 cultures maintained a normal cell cycle profile up to 72 hr (Figure 6D and E, respectively).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle distribution data in Figure 6D and E

claim: Upon prolonged mitogen starvation for more than 4 days, TKO and CyclinD1 RPE-1 cells started to die.
source: Upon prolonged mitogen starvation for more than 4 days, TKO and CyclinD1 cells started to die (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing cell death

claim: Cell death of mitogen-starved TKO and CyclinD1 RPE-1 cells could not be avoided by overexpression of Bcl2.
source: Cell death could not be avoided by overexpression of Bcl2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D and E)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data confirming Bcl2 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D) and microscopy images showing cell death (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E)

claim: Cell death of mitogen-starved TKO and CyclinD1 RPE-1 cells could not be avoided by additional inactivation of TP53.
source: Cell death could not be avoided by overexpression of Bcl2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D and E) nor by additional inactivation of TP53 (Figure 6F,G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data confirming p53 knockout (Figure 6F, G) and microscopy images showing cell death (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F)

claim: p53-proficient TKO-Bcl2 RPE-1s showed induction of DNA DSBs after one day of mitogen starvation.
source: Similar to TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, p53-proficient TKO-Bcl2 RPE-1s showed induction of DNA DSBs after one day of mitogen starvation. In contrast, no DSB induction was seen in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO RPE-1s (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 6H showing increased tail moments

claim: No DSB induction was seen in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO RPE-1s after one day of mitogen starvation.
source: Similar to TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, p53-proficient TKO-Bcl2 RPE-1s showed induction of DNA DSBs after one day of mitogen starvation. In contrast, no DSB induction was seen in TKO-Bcl2-p53KO RPE-1s (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 6H showing no increase in tail moments

claim: Mitogen starvation hardly induced DSBs in CyclinD1-Bcl2-p53KO RPE-1s compared to CyclinD1-Bcl2 RPE-1s.
source: Similarly, mitogen starvation hardly induced DSBs in CyclinD1-Bcl2-p53KO RPE-1s compared to CyclinD1-Bcl2 RPE-1s (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 6I showing minimal DSB induction in p53KO cells

claim: Mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 and CyclinD1-Bcl2 RPE-1s showed a decrease in the level origin firing.
source: Mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 and CyclinD1-Bcl2 RPE-1s showed a decrease in the level origin firing (Figure 6J,K).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 6J,K showing reduced origin firing

claim: TKO-Bcl2-p53KO and CyclinD1-Bcl2-p53KO RPE1-s maintained normal levels of origin firing after mitogen deprivation.
source: In contrast, TKO-Bcl2-p53KO and CyclinD1-Bcl2-p53KO RPE1-s maintained normal levels of origin firing after mitogen deprivation (Figure 6J,K)
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 6J,K showing maintained origin firing

claim: There is no difference in replication fork speed upon mitogen-deprivation in TKO-Bcl2 and TKO-Bcl2-p53KO RPE-1s.
source: In contrast, TKO-Bcl2-p53KO and CyclinD1-Bcl2-p53KO RPE1-s maintained normal levels of origin firing after mitogen deprivation (Figure 6J,K), although there is no difference in replication fork speed upon mitogen-deprivation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and F).
evidence: Supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and F

claim: Inactivation of p53 in G1/S phase checkpoint defective human cells reduced the accumulation of DNA DSBs following mitogen deprivation, possibly by rescuing the level of origin firing.
source: These results show that also in human cells inactivation of p53 in G1/S phase checkpoint defective cells reduced the accumulation of DNA DSBs following mitogen deprivation, possible by rescuing the level of origin firing.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of reduced DSBs and restored origin firing in human RPE-1 cells

claim: Murine retinoblastomas showed pronounced p53 and γ-H2AX staining.
source: Remarkably, murine retinoblastomas showed pronounced p53 and γ-H2AX staining (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 7A

claim: p53 appeared wild-type in a series of seven murine retinoblastomas by sequencing.
source: However, by sequencing, p53 appeared wild-type in a separate series of seven tumors, indicating that in this model retinoblastomas did activate the DDR but could still colonize the entire eyeball.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data mentioned in text

claim: In the murine retinoblastoma model, retinoblastomas activated the DDR but could still colonize the entire eyeball.
source: However, by sequencing, p53 appeared wild-type in a separate series of seven tumors, indicating that in this model retinoblastomas did activate the DDR but could still colonize the entire eyeball.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of DDR activation (γ-H2AX staining) and wild-type p53 in large tumors

claim: No chimeric animals were obtained from Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- ESCs.
source: However, no chimeric animals were obtained from Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- ESCs, likely indicating that combined ablation of the Rb and p53 pathways is incompatible with embryonic development.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation of failed chimera generation

claim: Combined ablation of the Rb and p53 pathways is likely incompatible with embryonic development.
source: However, no chimeric animals were obtained from Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- ESCs, likely indicating that combined ablation of the Rb and p53 pathways is incompatible with embryonic development.
evidence: Inferred from the failure to obtain chimeric animals from triple knockout ESCs

claim: Rb-/-Rbl2-/- ESCs developed a teratoma in 4 out of 6 mice.
source: Rb-/-Rbl2-/- ESCs developed a teratoma in 4 out of 6 mice; in contrast, Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- ESCs developed a tumor in 6 out of 6 injected mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from teratoma formation assay

claim: Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- ESCs developed a tumor in 6 out of 6 injected mice.
source: Rb-/-Rbl2-/- ESCs developed a teratoma in 4 out of 6 mice; in contrast, Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- ESCs developed a tumor in 6 out of 6 injected mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from teratoma formation assay

claim: On average the Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- tumors were larger than Rb-/-Rbl2-/- tumors.
source: On average the Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- tumors were larger than Rb-/-Rbl2-/- tumors (Figure 7B), although there is a 11% chance that the difference is accidental (p=0.1116, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by tumor weight data in Figure 7B, though statistical significance is marginal

claim: Teratomas of both Rb-/-Rbl2-/- and Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- genotypes mainly showed early neuronal differentiation and stained positive for γ-H2AX.
source: Teratomas of both genotypes mainly showed early neuronal differentiation and stained positive for the replication stress marker γ-H2AX (Figure 7C), suggesting that all tumors were suffering from replication stress.
evidence: Supported by histology and immunohistochemistry data in Figure 7C

claim: All teratomas were suffering from replication stress.
source: Teratomas of both genotypes mainly showed early neuronal differentiation and stained positive for the replication stress marker γ-H2AX (Figure 7C), suggesting that all tumors were suffering from replication stress.
evidence: Inferred from positive γ-H2AX staining in all tumors

claim: Three of the four Rb-/-Rbl2-/- teratomas showed an increase in tail moment compared to the tail moments of Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- teratomas.
source: Three of the four Rb-/-Rbl2-/- teratomas showed an increase in tail moment compared to the tail moments of Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- teratomas (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by comet assay data in Figure 7D

claim: The largest Rb-/-Rbl2-/- tumor had high levels of infiltrating neutrophils, which possibly explains its bigger size as well as the low level of DNA DSBs.
source: Of note, unlike the other tumors, the largest Rb-/-Rbl2-/- tumor (marked with asterisk in Figure 7B,D) had high levels of infiltrating neutrophils, which possibly explains its bigger size as well as the low level of DNA DSBs.
evidence: Observation of neutrophil infiltration with speculative explanation for outlier behavior

claim: p53 knockout teratomas showed a trend towards lower levels of DSBs and accelerated tumor growth.
source: Although the number of tumors was small, p53 knockout teratomas showed a trend towards lower levels of DSBs and accelerated tumor growth.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of tumor size and DSB level data, though sample size is limited

claim: Both in vitro and in vivo data suggest that inactivation of p53 in G1/S checkpoint deficient cells contributes to tumorigenesis by reducing DNA DSBs.
source: Therefore, both our in vitro as well as in vivo data suggest that inactivation of p53 in G1/S checkpoint deficient cells contributes to tumorigenesis by reducing DNA DSBs (Figure 7E).
evidence: Inferred from the combined in vitro and in vivo observations of reduced DSBs upon p53 loss

claim: Inactivation of p53 allowed mitogen-independent proliferation by restoring origin firing and reducing DNA breakage.
source: Inactivation of p53 allowed mitogen-independent proliferation, which remarkably was not only associated with alleviated G2 arrest but also with reduced DNA breakage and restored origin firing.
evidence: Supported by proliferation data (Figure 1), origin firing data (Figure 5C), and DSB data (Figure 3)

claim: The firing of origins requires Cyclin-CDK activity.
source: The firing of origins requires Cyclin-CDK activity (Fragkos et al., 2015; Méndez and Stillman, 2003).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations (Fragkos et al., 2015; Méndez and Stillman, 2003)

claim: In mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, CDK activity was low due to the high levels of p21Cip1 and p27Kip1.
source: In mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, CDK activity was low due to the high levels of p21Cip1 and p27Kip1 explaining the low level of origin firing.
evidence: Inferred from Western blot data showing high p21/p27 levels and previous work (Foijer et al., 2005) showing CDK inhibition

claim: Upon p53 inactivation, CDK activity likely increased and promoted origin firing.
source: It is therefore likely that upon p53 inactivation and therefore reduction of p21Cip1, CDK activity increased (Foijer et al., 2005) and hence promoted origin firing.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction of p21 upon p53 loss and previous work (Foijer et al., 2005) showing CDK activity restoration

claim: Genetic inactivation of p21Cip1 restored origin firing and promoted proliferation of mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs.
source: Consistently, we found that also genetic inactivation of p21Cip1 restored origin firing and promoted proliferation of mitogen-deprived TKO-Bcl2 MEFs.
evidence: Supported by origin firing data (Figure 5C) and proliferation data (Figure 1E) for p21KO cells

claim: Mitogen deprivation restricted origin firing and induced DNA breakage in G1/S-checkpoint-defective RPE-1s, and both could be reverted by inactivation of p53.
source: Importantly, this phenomenon was not restricted to murine cells, but also observed in human RPE-1 cells: mitogen deprivation restricted origin firing and induced DNA breakage in G1/S-checkpoint-defective RPE-1s, and both could be reverted by inactivation of p53.
evidence: Supported by origin firing data (Figure 6J,K) and DSB data (Figure 6H,I) in human RPE-1 cells

claim: RPE-1 cells appeared highly sensitive to apoptosis and therefore the damage-reducing effect of p53 loss did not translate into mitogen-independent proliferation.
source: However, for as yet unknown reasons, RPE-1 cells appeared highly sensitive to apoptosis and therefore the damage-reducing effect of p53 loss did not translate into mitogen-independent proliferation.
evidence: Supported by microscopy images showing cell death (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) despite p53 knockout

claim: KO of the p53 transcription target p21Cip1 phenocopied the effects of KO of p53 in TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, arguing against a transcription-independent role of p53 in suppressing DNA repair.
source: However, we show that KO of the p53 transcription target p21Cip1 phenocopied the effects of KO of p53 in TKO-Bcl2 MEFs, arguing against a transcription-independent role of p53 in suppressing DNA repair.
evidence: Inferred from the similar phenotypes of p53KO and p21KO cells (Figures 1, 3, 5)

claim: Increased DNA repair by NHEJ in G1 phase is unlikely as the levels of DSBs in serum-starved TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs remained low when G1 entry was prevented by artificially arresting cells in M-phase.
source: Furthermore, increased DNA repair by NHEJ in G1 phase is unlikely as the levels of DSBs in serum-starved TKO-Bcl2-p53KO MEFs remained low when G1 entry was prevented by artificially arresting cells in M-phase.
evidence: Supported by comet assay data with nocodazole treatment (Figure 3C)

claim: The accumulation of DNA DSBs in mitogen-deprived conditions can be attributed to loss of the G1/S phase checkpoint and not to other functions of the pRB protein or its family members.
source: We suggest that these other functions of pRB do not play a role in the accumulation of DNA damage in Rb-deficient cells since we observed the same phenotype in Rb-proficient Cyclin D1 overexpressing RPE-1s. Thus, the accumulation of DNA DSBs in mitogen-deprived conditions can be attributed to loss of the G1/S phase checkpoint and not to other functions of the pRB protein or its family members.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CyclinD1 overexpression (which bypasses Rb without losing Rb protein) produces the same phenotype

claim: Restoration of origin firing upon inactivation of p53, likely as a result of restored CDK activity, suppressed DNA breakage and allowed mitogen-independent proliferation.
source: As only origin firing but not replication speed was affected by p53 status, we favor a scenario where restoration of origin firing upon inactivation of p53, given the involvement of p21Cip1 likely as a result of restored CDK activity, suppressed DNA breakage and allowed mitogen-independent proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of restored origin firing, reduced DSBs, and continued proliferation in p53KO cells

claim: Loss of the Rb and p53 pathways frequently occur and co-occur in human tumors.
source: Loss of the Rb and p53 pathways frequently occur and co-occur in human tumors (Polager and Ginsberg, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Polager and Ginsberg, 2009)

claim: The p53 gene is mutated in more than 50% of human cancer.
source: The p53 gene is mutated in more than 50% of human cancer, and mutations in other genes that affect p53 function occur in many, if not all, tumors that retain a normal p53 gene (Perri et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Perri et al., 2016)

claim: Most human tumors lack the G1/S phase checkpoint.
source: In addition, most human tumors lack the G1/S phase checkpoint.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in cancer biology

claim: CCND1 represents the second most frequently amplified locus in the human cancer genome.
source: For example many human tumors overexpress D-type cyclins and CCND1 represents the second most frequently amplified locus in the human cancer genome (Hosokawa and Arnold, 1998; Menon and Povirk, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations (Hosokawa and Arnold, 1998; Menon and Povirk, 2014)

claim: The anti-apoptotic gene Bcl2 is commonly overexpressed in many types of cancer.
source: Furthermore, evading apoptosis is one of the hallmarks of cancer and the anti-apoptotic gene Bcl2, which is used in this study to suppress apoptosis, is commonly overexpressed in many types of cancer, including renal, prostate, gastric, lung and colorectal cancer, neuroblastoma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and acute and chronic leukemia (Frenzel et al., 2009; Kirkin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations (Frenzel et al., 2009; Kirkin et al., 2004)

claim: Approximately 90% of small cell lung cancer tumors have lost both p53 and Rb.
source: For example, approximately 90% of small cell lung cancer tumors have lost both p53 and Rb (Sekido et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation (Sekido et al., 2003)

claim: Small cell lung tumors are characterized by expression of Bcl2.
source: Beside this, small cell lung tumors are also characterized by expression of Bcl2 (Kaiser et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation (Kaiser et al., 1996)

claim: Human retinoblastoma originates from an intrinsic death-resistant precursor cell.
source: Furthermore, human retinoblastoma originates from an intrinsic death-resistant precursor cell (Xu et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation (Xu et al., 2009)

claim: Human retinoblastoma is characterized by mutations in the Rb gene.
source: Furthermore, human retinoblastoma originates from an intrinsic death-resistant precursor cell (Xu et al., 2009), is characterized by mutations in the Rb gene
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in cancer biology

claim: It is suggested that the p53 pathway is inactivated in human retinoblastoma.
source: Furthermore, human retinoblastoma originates from an intrinsic death-resistant precursor cell (Xu et al., 2009), is characterized by mutations in the Rb gene and it is suggested that the p53 pathway is inactivated (Xu et al., 2009; Laurie et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations (Xu et al., 2009; Laurie et al., 2006)

claim: The p53 pathway may be intrinsically attenuated upon RB1 loss by miR-24-mediated downregulation of p14ARF.
source: Although p53 mutations are infrequent in human retinoblastomas, the p53 pathway may be intrinsically attenuated upon RB1 loss by miR-24-mediated downregulation of p14ARF (To et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation (To et al., 2012)

claim: The p53 pathway may be attenuated by NANOS-mediated suppression of p53-activating kinases.
source: Although p53 mutations are infrequent in human retinoblastomas, the p53 pathway may be intrinsically attenuated upon RB1 loss by miR-24-mediated downregulation of p14ARF (To et al., 2012) and by NANOS-mediated suppression of p53-activating kinases (Miles et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation (Miles et al., 2014)

claim: RB1-deficient retinal cells may achieve attenuation of the p53 pathway by high expression of MDM2 and MDMX.
source: Other studies suggested that RB1-deficient retinal cells achieve attenuation of the p53 pathway by high expression of MDM2 and MDMX (Xu et al., 2009; Laurie et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations (Xu et al., 2009; Laurie et al., 2006)

claim: High MDM2 expression has critical p53-independent functions.
source: Other studies suggested that RB1-deficient retinal cells achieve attenuation of the p53 pathway by high expression of MDM2 and MDMX (Xu et al., 2009; Laurie et al., 2006), although a recent paper revealed critical p53-independent functions of high MDM2 expression (Qi and Cobrinik, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation (Qi and Cobrinik, 2017)

claim: When Rb was conditionally inactivated in retinal progenitor cells in a p107-/- background, non-invasive retinoblastomas developed with a penetrance of 60%.
source: When Rb was conditionally inactivated in retinal progenitor cells in a p107-/- background, non-invasive retinoblastomas developed with a penetrance of 60%. Upon additional inactivation of p53, aggressive, invasive bilateral retinoblastomas developed with 100% penetrance and reduced latency (Dyer et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations (Dyer et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2004)

claim: Upon additional inactivation of p53 in Rb/p107 deficient retinal progenitor cells, aggressive, invasive bilateral retinoblastomas developed with 100% penetrance and reduced latency.
source: Upon additional inactivation of p53, aggressive, invasive bilateral retinoblastomas developed with 100% penetrance and reduced latency (Dyer et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations (Dyer et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2004)

claim: Evidence has been obtained that murine retinoblastomas originate from an intrinsically death-resistant cell of origin.
source: Importantly, evidence has been obtained that murine retinoblastomas originate from an intrinsically death-resistant cell of origin (Chen et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation (Chen et al., 2004)

claim: The tumor promoting effect of attenuated p53 activity was not due to abrogation of an apoptotic response but rather required for maintaining sufficient CDK activity to counteract the deleterious effects of replication stress.
source: We therefore propose that the tumor promoting effect of attenuated p53 activity was not due to abrogation of an apoptotic response but rather required for maintaining sufficient CDK activity to counteract the deleterious effects of replication stress.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p53 loss reduces DSBs by restoring origin firing via CDK activity

claim: Tumor size was inversely correlated with the level of DNA breaks in the teratoma model.
source: We obtained support for such tumor-promoting effect of p53 ablation in an Rb-/-Rbl2-/- teratoma model: tumor size was inversely correlated with the level of DNA breaks
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of tumor weight and tail moment data (Figure 7C)

claim: Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- teratomas generally showed lower levels of DNA breaks than Rb-/-Rbl2-/- teratomas.
source: We obtained support for such tumor-promoting effect of p53 ablation in an Rb-/-Rbl2-/- teratoma model: tumor size was inversely correlated with the level of DNA breaks and Rb-/-Rbl2-/-p53-/- teratomas generally showed lower levels of DNA breaks than Rb-/-Rbl2-/- teratomas.
evidence: Supported by comet assay data from teratomas (Figure 7D)

claim: Oncogene activation can directly cause replication stress by hyper-stimulating DNA replication, which activates the ATR-Chk1 axis.
source: It has been suggested that oncogene activation can directly cause replication stress by hyper-stimulating DNA replication, which activates the ATR-Chk1 axis (Hills and Diffley, 2014; Di Micco et al., 2006; Halazonetis et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations (Hills and Diffley, 2014; Di Micco et al., 2006; Halazonetis et al., 2008)

claim: Frequent DNA breakage associated with replication stress activates the ATM-Chk2-p53 module that provides a strong barrier to proliferation by inducing apoptosis or permanent cell cycle arrest.
source: Furthermore, frequent DNA breakage associated with replication stress activates the complementary ATM-Chk2-p53 module that provides a strong barrier to proliferation by inducing apoptosis or permanent cell cycle arrest.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in DNA damage response

claim: Activation of the DDR may explain the strong selective pressure for loss of p53 in human cancer.
source: It has therefore been suggested that activation of the DDR may explain the strong selective pressure for loss of p53 in human cancer (Halazonetis et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation (Halazonetis et al., 2008)

claim: Replication stress in the authors' system was the consequence of the combination of Rb-protein deficiency and growth-restricting conditions, leading to DNA breakage and activation of the DDR.
source: Rather than a direct consequence of oncogene activation, replication stress in our system was the consequence of the combination of Rb-protein deficiency (hyper-activating E2F transcription factors) and growth-restricting conditions (the absence of mitogenic signaling), leading to DNA breakage and activation of the DDR.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design and observations throughout the study

claim: Loss of p53 not only abrogated cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, but also suppressed the induction of DNA damage itself.
source: Furthermore, we found loss of p53 not only abrogated cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, but also suppressed the induction of DNA damage itself, providing a novel mechanistic explanation for the frequent co-occurrence of p53 and pRb pathway inactivation in cancer.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental observations showing reduced DSB formation upon p53 loss

claim: Loss of p53 provides a novel mechanistic explanation for the frequent co-occurrence of p53 and pRb pathway inactivation in cancer.
source: Furthermore, we found loss of p53 not only abrogated cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, but also suppressed the induction of DNA damage itself, providing a novel mechanistic explanation for the frequent co-occurrence of p53 and pRb pathway inactivation in cancer.
evidence: Inferred from the findings that p53 loss reduces DSBs in Rb-deficient cells
